stemHtml: Q 03: A 34-year-old woman comes to your clinic complaining of persistent itching and thick, scaly plaques on her scalp for the past few months. On examination, the lesions are well-demarcated and confined to the scalp, with no involvement of the face, trunk, or extremities. She has no history of systemic illness. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment for her condition? (Question Id: 515019)
keywords: “Thick, scaly plaques on scalp” – indicates localized plaque-type psoriasis, pointing toward topical treatment.
“Confined to the scalp / no lesions elsewhere” – highlights limited disease, suggesting first-line therapy should be topical, not systemic.
“Persistent itching” – supports active inflammation but still mild-to-moderate severity, reinforcing topical corticosteroids as appropriate.
Reasoning: The keywords emphasize localized scalp involvement with mild-to-moderate severity, which directly guides toward topical corticosteroid shampoo as first-line therapy.
keywordsHtml:
1. “Thick, scaly plaques on scalp” – indicates localized plaque-type psoriasis, pointing toward topical treatment.
  2. “Confined to the scalp / no lesions elsewhere” – highlights limited disease, suggesting first-line therapy should be topical, not systemic.
  3. “Persistent itching” – supports active inflammation but still mild-to-moderate severity, reinforcing topical corticosteroids as appropriate.
Reasoning: The keywords emphasize localized scalp involvement with mild-to-moderate severity, which directly guides toward topical corticosteroid shampoo as first-line therapy.

B.title: Topical corticosteroid shampoo
B.body:
Topical corticosteroid shampoos (such as clobetasol propionate) are considered the first-line treatment for localized scalp psoriasis. The scalp skin is relatively thick, which allows for the use of high-potency corticosteroids with a lower risk of skin atrophy compared to the face.
Shampoos or foams are preferred over ointments in this area because they are easier to apply through the hair and have better patient compliance.
They work by reducing the underlying inflammation and slowing down the rapid skin cell turnover that causes plaque formation.
Reduces inflammation, erythema, and scaling effectively.
Safe for short- to medium-term use, can be combined with keratolytic agents like salicylic acid if thick plaques are present.
B.bodyHtml:
• Topical corticosteroid shampoos (such as clobetasol propionate) are considered the first-line treatment for localized scalp psoriasis. The scalp skin is relatively thick, which allows for the use of high-potency corticosteroids with a lower risk of skin atrophy compared to the face.
  • Shampoos or foams are preferred over ointments in this area because they are easier to apply through the hair and have better patient compliance.
  • They work by reducing the underlying inflammation and slowing down the rapid skin cell turnover that causes plaque formation.
  • Reduces inflammation, erythema, and scaling effectively.
  • Safe for short- to medium-term use, can be combined with keratolytic agents like salicylic acid if thick plaques are present.

A.title: Oral methotrexate
A.body:
Systemic immunosuppressant used for moderate-to-severe psoriasis or extensive disease.
Not first-line for limited, mild scalp psoriasis due to risk of systemic side effects.
A.bodyHtml:
• Systemic immunosuppressant used for moderate-to-severe psoriasis or extensive disease.
  • Not first-line for limited, mild scalp psoriasis due to risk of systemic side effects.

C.title: Phototherapy
C.body:
Effective for generalized psoriasis, especially plaque-type.
Not practical or necessary for localized scalp involvement only.
C.bodyHtml:
• Effective for generalized psoriasis, especially plaque-type.
  • Not practical or necessary for localized scalp involvement only.

D.title: Oral acitretin
D.body:
Systemic retinoid for severe or refractory psoriasis.
Avoided in localized disease due to potential hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity, and mucocutaneous side effects.
D.bodyHtml:
• Systemic retinoid for severe or refractory psoriasis.
  • Avoided in localized disease due to potential hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity, and mucocutaneous side effects.

E.title: Biologic therapy
E.body:
Reserved for severe, extensive, or refractory psoriasis affecting quality of life.
Not indicated in mild, localized scalp psoriasis.
E.bodyHtml:
• Reserved for severe, extensive, or refractory psoriasis affecting quality of life.
  • Not indicated in mild, localized scalp psoriasis.

keyConcept:
Localized scalp psoriasis should initially be treated with topical therapy, preferably corticosteroid shampoo.
Systemic therapy is reserved for extensive, severe, or refractory cases.
Treatment choice depends on disease severity, extent, and site rather than patient age or duration alone.
keyConceptHtml:
• Localized scalp psoriasis should initially be treated with topical therapy, preferably corticosteroid shampoo.
  • Systemic therapy is reserved for extensive, severe, or refractory cases.
  • Treatment choice depends on disease severity, extent, and site rather than patient age or duration alone.

diagram.name: Scalp Psoriasis – First-Line Management
diagram.caption: The diagram illustrates mild-to-moderate, localized scalp psoriasis with thick, scaly plaques. It highlights topical corticosteroid shampoo as the first-line treatment, supported by keratolytic agents to remove scales. It also emphasizes avoiding systemic therapies like oral medications, phototherapy, or biologics in mild, localized cases. Visual labels clearly show key features, treatment, and adjunct measures
